Same code, about 62% more output tokens: Claude vs GPT vs Gemini in four coding tools and five languages

Measured and written by Jonhisking · Updated 2026-10-24. Disclosure: TokenSave gets no funding, credits or sponsorship from AI companies. All measurements use our own paid subscriptions.

To write the same kind of game, Claude Opus 5.5 spent about 62% more output tokens per character of code than Gemini 4 Argon, and about 57% more than GPT. Opus came out the same in Claude Code (591 tokens per 1,000 characters) and in Google’s Antigravity CLI (602), so it is the model, not the tool. Counting the same 76 game files with all three tokenizers shows why: Claude’s tokenizer needs 55% more tokens than GPT’s for the same code and 29% more than Gemini’s. Writing the prompt in Korean, Japanese, Spanish or Ukrainian instead of English changed input tokens by only a few percent.

Measured 2026-10-18 to 2026-10-23 · 100 runs · Claude Code 2.1.295, Codex CLI 0.162, Antigravity CLI 1.4.5 · License CC BY 4.0

DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23585139 · Also on Hugging Face · Kaggle · GitHub

Key findings

  • Output tokens per 1,000 characters of game code: Opus 5.5 591 in Claude Code and 602 in Antigravity, Gemini 4 Argon 372, gpt-6-luna 376 in Codex. The range across the five prompt languages was narrow for every model (Opus 554 to 624, Gemini 363 to 382, GPT 366 to 386).
  • Why it matters: output tokens are the expensive ones (Opus 5.5 charges five times more for output than for input), and because the gap is per character, it comes on top of any difference in how long each model’s game turned out. It matches the direction of our earlier tokenizer test, where the same source code needed 43% to 59% more Claude tokens than GPT tokens.
  • Prompt language barely moved input tokens. Inside each tool the five languages stayed within a few percent; the tool decided the size: about 78,638 input tokens in Claude Code, 48,538 in Codex and 11,671 to 13,437 in Antigravity for the Korean prompt. Most of every request is the tool’s own instructions.
  • Opus wrote longer games in Korean and Ukrainian in Antigravity (10,057 and 9,692 characters against 7,749 in English), so its total output rose there, but per character it stayed the same.
  • 99 of 100 games worked (score rises, level 2 appears, lives go 3, 2, 1, 0), and every game showed its text in the prompt language. The one failure is a Codex game from the earlier dataset.

Tokenizer check: the same files, three tokenizers (v1.2)

On 2026-10-24 we counted 76 of the game files with each company’s own tokenizer, regardless of which model wrote them. Tokens per 1,000 characters, median per group. “Output beyond the code” = reported output tokens divided by the file counted with the writing model’s own tokenizer (the final reply and tool-call wrapping).

Code written byClaude 5.5 tokenizerGemini 4 Argon tokenizerGPT (o200k) tokenizerReported outputOutput beyond the code
Claude Code + Opus 5.5 (23 files)512399334574+14%
Antigravity + Opus 5.5 (15 files)524414343593+13%
Antigravity + Gemini 4 Argon (15 files)451346290371+7%
Codex + gpt-6-luna (23 files)534407338378+11%
  • Same code, different counts. Across all 76 files Claude’s tokenizer needed 55% more tokens than GPT’s (every file between +47% and +65%) and 29% more than Gemini’s (+24% to +35%).
  • Against GPT, the gap is the tokenizer. Opus and GPT wrote code of about the same token density and added a similar amount beyond the code, so almost all of the difference in output per character comes from how Claude splits text.
  • Against Gemini, the tokenizer explains about half. The rest: Gemini’s own code needed 13% to 15% fewer tokens per character than the other models’ code under all three tokenizers, and it added less beyond the code.

Method

  • Task: “Make a brick-breaker game that runs in the browser as a single file named index.html … 2 levels, a score display and 3 lives … keyboard and mouse”, translated into Korean, Japanese, Spanish and Ukrainian. Medium effort everywhere, each run in its own empty folder on Windows 11.
  • Claude Code 2.1.295 and Codex CLI 0.162: the 50 runs of our prompt-language dataset (2026-10-18 and 19). Antigravity CLI 1.4.5: English runs 1 to 3 from our three-way comparison (2026-10-22), the other 44 runs new (2026-10-23; runs 4 and 5 in every language added the same day).
  • Every game was played in headless Chromium by a script that watches the score, the level and the lives; the check reads the game’s own text in all five languages.
  • Tokenizer check: Claude 5.5 counted with Claude Code (claude -p, Haiku 5.5, which shares Opus 5.5’s tokenizer; no tools, no MCP; minus the same call with “a”), Gemini 4 Argon with the Google AI Studio token counter (minus 31, the count for “a” is 32), GPT with o200k locally. Repeating the first file gave identical counts. The 76 files are the runs whose game files are stored in our repository. Per-file counts: tokenizer check CSV.

Limitations

  • Output tokens include the short final reply and the tool-call wrapping around the file, not only the code. Antigravity reported no or few thinking tokens; Claude Code and Codex count any reasoning inside their output figure.
  • One task (a browser game in HTML, CSS and JavaScript). Other kinds of code may tokenize differently.
  • 3 to 5 runs per cell, measured over six days with the same tool versions.
